title: Lower temperature sensitivity, not detection loss, explains why animal first dates advanced less than plant spring dates in ex-USSR nature reserves, 1948-2018
abstract: Question: do animal first dates in the Chronicles of Nature Calendar (ex-USSR nature reserves) contain the detection bias found in the Japan JMA network, and does this bias or a lower temperature sensitivity explain why consumer spring dates advanced less than plant spring dates? Approach: we used 1948-2018 records with quality OK, local temperature from GHCN-CAMS (CRU TS check), the JMA definitions of non-detected neighbour years, fixed-effects models clustered by site, a sign test with autumn last dates, a fixed-cohort record share and a decomposition of trends into sensitivity x warming plus a residual. Results: animal first dates were 2.2 days later (95% CI 1.1 to 3.4) per unit share of non-detected neighbour years (Japan 5.8); plant onset dates had 0.8 (-0.1 to 1.7). The animal link came only from earlier neighbour years, disappeared with series x decade fixed effects (0.4) and was smaller than the plant link in three of four regions. Autumn last dates were not earlier near non-detection years (+2.3; -0.7 to 5.3). The bird record share went from about 0.90 to 0.79-0.84 (Japan 0.89 to 0.57). Consumer first dates advanced -0.44 days per decade and plant spring dates -0.89 in 1948-2018. The consumer lag of +0.44 (0.17 to 0.69) equals the lower consumer sensitivity (-1.2 versus -2.8 days per C) times warming (+0.57; 0.38 to 0.73); the residual difference was -0.13 (-0.36 to 0.12), also for 1960-2018 and 30-120 day windows. Temperature-controlled consumer dates did not move later (+0.05 days per decade). In 1986-2018 birds advanced 0.72 days per decade more than local warming predicts. Conclusion: the consumer lag in these reserves is not a detection artefact; it follows from lower temperature sensitivity. Limitations: missing records mix non-detection, observer change and digitization; only 41 sites enter the detection model; the last-date test has 17 sites; no abundance data.
